text: CHOOSE does one specific job: pick a value out of a list by its position. Give it an index first, then the list of candidates, and it returns whichever one sits at that spot -- counting from 1, not from 0.

Here's a realistic use. SalesOrderHeader stores order status as a small numeric code, 1 through 6. CHOOSE turns that code straight into a readable label in one line -- status 1 picks In Process, status 5 picks Shipped, each one lining up with its position in the list.

What happens past the end of the list? Unlike an array access that might throw an error in other languages, CHOOSE just returns NULL. No exception, nothing that stops the batch -- it quietly tells you there's nothing at that position.

But keep its scope in mind. CHOOSE can only pick by numeric position -- it has no way to test a condition like whether a price is over a thousand dollars. For anything beyond a direct index-to-value lookup, CASE is still the tool you reach for.
One more thing worth confirming for yourself: CHOOSE is strictly 1-based. Index 0 doesn't point anywhere valid either, so it returns NULL too, same as any other out-of-range index.
Next up, we move from conditional shortcuts to data safety: TRY_CAST and TRY_CONVERT, which let you attempt a conversion without crashing the whole batch when the data doesn't cooperate.
